Online Matching in Convex Bipartite Graphs

Yilong Feng    Zhihao Gavin Tang    Kangning Wang    Xiaowei Wu
September 4, 2026
Abstract

Online resource-allocation systems, like outpatient scheduling and spectrum allocation, often assign sequentially arriving requests to an ordered pool of scarce resources, where each request accepts a contiguous interval of feasible options. We study the resulting online matching problem on convex bipartite graphs under irrevocable decisions and adversarial arrivals. We first show that convexity alone does not improve the classic worst-case guarantee of 1−1/e1-1/e, achieved by Ranking. We then consider the uniform-length model, in which every online request has exactly dd consecutive offline neighbors. We propose Flip, which uses one random bit to commit ex-ante to either earliest-feasible assignment or latest-feasible assignment. Although either natural deterministic policy can waste capacity and be asymptotically only 1/21/2-competitive, we show that their randomized mixture is 2/32/3-competitive. This guarantee is tight for Flip and remains valid against a semi-adaptive adversary that observes the selected policy before choosing the arrival order. We also prove that no randomized online algorithm can achieve a competitive ratio strictly larger than 3/43/4 in the uniform-length model.

1 Introduction

Online bipartite matching is a fundamental model for allocating resources to sequentially arriving requests. It has been studied extensively since the seminal work of Karp, Vazirani, and Vazirani [21]. A set of offline resources is known in advance, whereas online requests arrive one at a time and reveal their compatible resources only upon arrival. Each request must be matched immediately and irrevocably to an available compatible resource, or be left unmatched. The objective is to maximize the size of the final matching. The performance of an online algorithm is typically measured by its competitive ratio, defined as the worst-case ratio between its expected matching size and the size of a maximum matching. For general bipartite graphs, any greedy algorithm that matches a request whenever possible is 1/21/2-competitive, and no deterministic algorithm can guarantee a better ratio. The celebrated Ranking algorithm achieves the optimal randomized ratio of 1−1/e1-1/e against the standard oblivious adversary [21].

These worst-case guarantees make no structural assumptions about the compatibility graph. In many operations-research applications, however, the offline resources possess a natural order and the compatibility constraints have additional structure. The offline side represents a fixed stock of resources, and the system operator seeks to use this capacity efficiently by serving as many requests as possible. The online side represents demand revealed sequentially: each request seeks an acceptable resource, but its feasible choices are restricted by operational requirements or service preferences. Because decisions are irrevocable and future requests are unknown, each assignment carries an opportunity cost; choosing which compatible resource to allocate is therefore central to the overall service level and system throughput.

Consider, for example, a platform that allocates a fixed set of time slots over a planning horizon. Each requester is willing to accept any slot within its acceptable time window, while the platform seeks to accommodate as many requests as possible. This captures outpatient scheduling, where hospitals allocate remaining appointment capacity to patients with time preferences [15]. The same pattern appears in airport slot allocation, where an airline requests a preferred takeoff or landing time but may accept another time within a displacement window [29, 14]. A similar setting arises in spectrum allocation. A licensed frequency band is divided into ordered channels, and assignments must account for channel availability and interference between nearby frequencies [1]. Spectrum requests may also arrive online and require immediate, non-preemptive admission decisions [28]. In a simple stylized model, each device has a preferred channel and can use that channel or a fixed number of nearby channels. If the same displacement limit applies to every device, all acceptable frequency ranges have the same length. In all these applications, the resources are ordered, and the resources acceptable to each request are consecutive in that order.

Compatibility graphs with this consecutive-neighborhood property belong to the class of convex bipartite graphs [18]. A bipartite graph is convex on one side if the vertices on that side admit a linear order in which the neighborhood of every vertex on the opposite side is consecutive. We assume convexity on the offline side, and the offline order is known to the online algorithm in advance. We refer to the resulting online neighborhoods as interval neighborhoods.

This gives rise to the following natural question:

Can convexity on the offline side be exploited to beat 1−1/e1-1/e for online bipartite matching?

1.1 Our Results

Perhaps surprisingly, we show that convexity alone does not improve the worst-case service guarantee. When request intervals may have arbitrary lengths, the optimal competitive ratio remains 1−1/e1-1/e.

Theorem 1.1.

No algorithm has a competitive ratio strictly larger than 1−1/e1-1/e for online matching in convex bipartite graphs.

Recall that Ranking is (1−1/e)(1-1/e)-competitive on general bipartite graphs, so this upper bound is tight. At a high level, our construction reproduces the upper-triangular structure of the classic 1−1/e1-1/e hard instance by recursively replacing each offline resource with a sufficiently large block of consecutive resources. Every request then has an interval of feasible resources, but these intervals have widely varying lengths. From an operations perspective, this result shows that an ordered capacity structure does not by itself protect the system from worst-case congestion: sufficiently heterogeneous flexibility across requests can recreate the same bottlenecks as in an unstructured compatibility graph.

Many applications, however, standardize the amount of flexibility offered to each request. A scheduling platform may require every acceptable time window to contain the same number of slots; similarly, an airport or spectrum-allocation system may impose a common displacement tolerance. Besides simplifying the service design, such a restriction provides a basic form of procedural fairness across customers. Motivated by these settings, we study the uniform-length model, in which every request can be assigned to exactly dd consecutive resources, for some d≥2d\geq 2. We show that this restriction fundamentally changes the attainable service level: the 1−1/e1-1/e barrier can be surpassed by a transparent randomized policy using only one random bit.

To explain the policy, recall a useful offline property of convex bipartite graphs. For each online vertex vv, let s⁡(v)s(v) and l⁡(v)l(v) denote the smallest and largest indices in its interval neighborhood, respectively. When all requests are known in advance, a maximum matching can be obtained by processing requests in non-decreasing order of l⁡(v)l(v) and assigning each request to its smallest-indexed available resource. Symmetrically, one may process requests in non-increasing order of s⁡(v)s(v) and assign each request to its largest-indexed available resource [18]. In the online system, the arrival sequence is exogenous, but the operator can retain the corresponding resource-selection decisions. This yields two natural dispatching policies:

  • •

    The up-matching rule is an earliest-feasible assignment policy: assign each arriving request to its smallest-indexed currently available feasible resource.

  • •

    The down-matching rule is a latest-feasible assignment policy: assign each arriving request to its largest-indexed currently available feasible resource.

Both policies are work-conserving in the sense that they serve a request whenever any compatible capacity remains, and neither policy requires demand forecasts or knowledge of future arrivals. Nevertheless, each policy has a systematic directional bias and can waste capacity badly: it may consume resources that are critical for later requests while leaving residual capacity that subsequent demand cannot use. Each rule always produces a maximal matching and is therefore 1/21/2-competitive. The examples in Figure 1 show that this poor performance guarantee is essentially tight. In each instance, the indicated policy serves only dd requests, whereas a clairvoyant scheduler serves 2​d−12d-1. The resulting ratio is d2​d−1\frac{d}{2d-1}, which converges to 1/21/2 as d→∞d\to\infty. Thus, neither earliest-feasible nor latest-feasible assignment provides a satisfactory worst-case service guarantee when used alone.

The two instances also reveal the complementarity of the policies. On the left instance, latest-feasible assignment wastes substantial capacity, whereas earliest-feasible assignment attains the offline optimum; on the right instance, the roles are reversed. We therefore propose Flip, which makes a single ex-ante random choice between the two policies. Before any request arrives, Flip samples a fair coin, commits to either the earliest-feasible or latest-feasible assignment, and follows that policy throughout the planning horizon. Thus, the algorithm randomizes over two stable dispatching policies rather than making a new randomized decision for every request. It uses only one random bit and does not require dd as an input.

This simple policy mixture provides a robust service-level guarantee. For every uniform-length instance, its expected number of served requests is at least 2​d−13​d−2\frac{2d-1}{3d-2} times the number served by a clairvoyant optimal scheduler. Moreover, our analysis holds against a semi-adaptive adversary: the compatibility graph is fixed first, the adversary then observes which of the two policies Flip has selected, and only afterward chooses the arrival order. The adversary may therefore use a different policy-aware worst-case sequence for each outcome of the coin flip. Consequently, the guarantee does not rely on concealing the selected dispatching rule; the operator may announce and consistently apply the policy before operations begin. This public-commitment interpretation is stronger than the standard oblivious-adversary model and is particularly relevant in settings where assignment rules must be transparent to customers or regulators. The policy is also operationally lightweight: A standard balanced ordered-set data structure implements either policy in O⁡(log⁡m)O(\log m) time per arrival using O⁡(m)O(m) space, where mm is the number of offline resources. Hence Flip is not only analytically simple but also easy to deploy at scale.

Theorem 1.2.

Algorithm Flip is 2​d−13​d−2\frac{2d-1}{3d-2}-competitive for online matching in uniform-length convex bipartite graphs, even against the semi-adaptive adversary described above, and the ratio is tight for Flip.

To benchmark the value of more sophisticated online controls, we complement this guarantee with an impossibility result that applies to every randomized assignment policy in the uniform-length model.

Theorem 1.3.

No algorithm has a competitive ratio strictly larger than 3/43/4 for online matching in uniform-length convex bipartite graphs.

Consequently, the optimal worst-case service ratio in the uniform-length setting lies in [2/3,3/4][2/3,3/4]. The lower endpoint is achieved asymptotically by the one-bit Flip policy, while the upper endpoint limits what any online policy can guarantee.

1.2 Our Techniques

We next outline the proof of the competitive guarantee for Flip.

From Oblivious Adversary to Semi-adaptive Adversary.

Let M⋆M^{\star} be the maximum matching derived by the offline greedy procedure that processes online vertices in non-decreasing order of l⁡(v)l(v) [18]. We first show that it suffices to consider the instances where M⋆M^{\star} covers all nn online vertices. Thus |M⋆|=n|M^{\star}|=n. We index the online vertices as v1,v2,…,vnv_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{n} according to the order in which the offline greedy procedure processes them. We analyze the performance of Flip against a semi-adaptive adversary11 1 As Figure 1 shows, Flip is only 1/21/2-competitive against a fully-adaptive adversary. that first fixes the underlying graph, then sees the rule chosen by the algorithm, and finally decides the online arrival order. In particular, it may choose different arrival orders for the two outcomes of the random bit. This adversary is stronger than the standard oblivious adversary. Thus, any guarantee against it also holds against the oblivious adversary. We show that among all arrival orders, the up-matching rule attains its minimum matching size on the order vn,vn−1,…,v1v_{n},v_{n-1},\ldots,v_{1}, whereas the down-matching rule attains its minimum on the order v1,v2,…,vnv_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{n}. It therefore suffices to analyze these two canonical orders.

Encoding Unmatched Vertices to Bad Indices of an Offset Function.

The maximum matching M⋆M^{\star} allows us to encode the instance by a one-dimensional discrete function ff. Let sis_{i} be the smallest index of the ii-th interval and let μi\mu_{i} be the index of the offline vertex matched to it by M⋆M^{\star}. Let f⁡(i):=μi−si+1f(i):=\mu_{i}-s_{i}+1, which denotes the number of neighbors of viv_{i} with index at most μi\mu_{i}. We call ff the offset function, as f⁡(i)f(i) records the offset between the highest-priority neighbor of viv_{i} under the up-matching rule and the perfect neighbor of viv_{i} in M⋆M^{\star}. By definition, we have f⁡(i)∈[d]f(i)\in[d] for all i∈[n]i\in[n]. We further show that f⁡(i+1)≤f⁡(i)+1f(i+1)\leq f(i)+1, e.g., ff grows at a rate of at most 11. Most importantly, we provide the necessary conditions for online vertices to be unmatched using the offset function. In particular, an online vertex left unmatched by the down-matching rule can occur only at an index whose ff-value is strictly larger than those at the preceding dd indices, i.e., viv_{i} is unmatched only if

f⁡(i)>f⁡(j),∀j∈[i−d,i−1].f(i)>f(j),\qquad\forall j\in[i-d,i-1].

Symmetrically, an online vertex left unmatched by the up-matching rule can occur only at an index whose ff-value is strictly smaller than those at the following dd indices. We refer to these local extrema as bad indices, and let HH be the set of bad indices for down-matching, and LL be that for up-matching. Since only vertices corresponding to bad indices can be unmatched, lower bounding the competitive ratio reduces to upper bounding the total number of bad indices:

|H|+|L|≤2​d−23​d−2⋅n.|H|+|L|\leq\frac{2d-2}{3d-2}\cdot n. (1)

Charging Argument for Bounding the Bad Indices.

Intuitively, there cannot be too many bad indices. If ii is an HH-bad index, then f⁡(i)f(i) is larger than the values at all dd preceding indices. If one of these preceding indices is also HH-bad, then its value must in turn exceed the values at its own dd preceding indices. Consequently, along any sequence of HH-bad indices in which consecutive indices are at distance at most dd, the corresponding function values are strictly increasing. We call such a sequence a chain of bad indices. We show that every chain has length at most d−1d-1 and that any two maximal chains are separated by at least dd indices. This immediately gives the upper bound d−12​d−1⋅n\frac{d-1}{2d-1}\cdot n on the number of indices in HH. The same upper bound holds for LL. Although each bound can be tight individually, as witnessed by Figure 1, a strictly better bound holds for |H|+|L||H|+|L|. However, this relies on a careful handling of the interactions between HH-chains and LL-chains. The key interaction lemma shows that when an HH-chain of length xx and an LL-chain of length yy are within a distance of at most 2​d2d, then their total length is at most d−1d-1. We convert this local restriction into a global charging argument by assigning a proxy of indices to every maximal chain. The length of a proxy of a chain is proportional to the length of the chain. Proxies associated with chains of the same type are disjoint. The proxies are constructed so that an intersection between two proxies of opposite types implies x+y≤d−1x+y\leq d-1, which allows us to pack all proxies within a space of size nn. By upper bounding the total length of proxies and using the symmetry between HH and LL, we prove Equation (1), which then yields a competitive ratio of 2​d−13​d−2\frac{2d-1}{3d-2}.

1.3 Other Related Work

Due to the vast literature on online bipartite matching, we review only the most relevant studies here. For broader surveys, we refer to Mehta [23] and the more recent survey of Huang et al. [19].

Online Matching with Bounded Degree.

A major line of work obtains better guarantees for online bipartite matching by exploiting the graph’s degree structure. Buchbinder et al. [8] considered graphs with maximum online degree dd and proposed a deterministic fractional algorithm with competitive ratio 1−(1−1/d)d1-(1-1/d)^{d}. Azar et al. [5] proved a matching impossibility result for deterministic fractional algorithms. Naor and Wajc [24] introduced (k,d)(k,d)-bounded graphs in which offline vertices have degrees at least kk while online vertices have degrees at most dd with k≥d≥2k\geq d\geq 2, and gave an optimal deterministic algorithm with a competitive ratio of 1−(1−1/d)k1-(1-1/d)^{k}. For dd-regular graphs, Cohen and Wajc [11] designed a randomized algorithm whose competitive ratio tends to 11 as dd grows. Note that our uniform-length setting imposes no nontrivial bound on the offline degrees; it is therefore incomparable with both (k,d)(k,d)-boundedness and regularity. Further work has studied different degree regimes, vertex capacities, and related allocation problems [4, 3, 10, 16]. More recently, Bhangale et al. [6] determined the optimal randomized competitive ratio of approximately 0.71780.7178 when each online vertex has degree at most 22.

Convex and Geometric Matching.

Glover [18] introduced convex bipartite graphs and showed that a maximum matching can be obtained by a greedy rule. Lipski and Preparata [20] gave near-linear and linear-time algorithms for convex and doubly convex graphs, respectively. Subsequent works [17, 25] further reduced the time complexity, resulting in an O⁡(|V|)O(|V|)-time algorithm by Steiner and Yeomans [27]. Katriel [22] studied the vertex-weighted variant of convex bipartite matching and related it to scheduling unit-length jobs with release times and deadlines. Brodal et al. [7] studied the dynamic maintenance of maximum matchings in convex bipartite graphs. Abels et al. [2] studied an online-over-time variant on interval-constrained bipartite graphs, allowing previously matched online vertices to be reassigned to later time slots. Sentenac et al. [26] considered one-dimensional bipartite random geometric graphs; these graphs are doubly convex when both sides are ordered by location. Unlike the former model, ours permits no reassignment; unlike the latter, we seek worst-case guarantees under adversarial graphs and arrival orders.

Max-min Greedy Matching.

Analyzing Flip against the semi-adaptive adversary is closely related to the max-min greedy matching problem introduced by Eden et al. [13]. Given a bipartite graph with a perfect matching of size nn, a max player first chooses a priority order on the offline vertices; a min player then chooses a worst-case arrival order of the online side. Eden et al. [13] showed that the max player can always guarantee a matching size of at least 0.51⋅n0.51\cdot n. Importantly, the priority order chosen by the max player may depend on the graph. Eden et al. [13] showed that a uniformly random priority order gets an expected matching size of only (0.5+o⁡(1))⋅n(0.5+o(1))\cdot n in the worst case. In our uniform-length setting, Flip and the semi-adaptive adversary follow the same order of play. However, Flip randomizes only between two graph-independent priority orders: the increasing and decreasing orders of the offline vertices. Nevertheless, we show that the average of their worst-case matching sizes is at least 2/3⋅n2/3\cdot n whenever each online vertex is adjacent to exactly dd consecutive offline vertices. In contrast to general bipartite graphs, the convex structure on the offline side therefore makes it possible to obtain a guarantee above 0.50.5 using priority orders that are independent of the graph. On the negative side, Cohen-Addad et al. [12] observed that there exists a graph for which every priority order has a worst-case matching size of at most 2/3⋅n2/3\cdot n. Chan et al. [9] established strong conditional hardness results for computing an optimal response of the min player to a given priority order.

2 Preliminaries

Notations.

We write [k][k] for {1,2,…,k}\{1,2,\ldots,k\} and [a,b][a,b] for {a,a+1,…,b}\{a,a+1,\ldots,b\}.

Let G=(U∪V,E)G=(U\cup V,E) be a bipartite graph, where U={u1,…,um}U=\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{m}\} is the set of offline vertices and V={v1,…,vn}V=\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{n}\} is the set of online vertices. The offline vertices, together with their order u1,u2,…,umu_{1},u_{2},\ldots,u_{m}, are known to the algorithm in advance. The online vertices arrive one at a time in an adversarial order. Upon the arrival of an online vertex vv, the algorithm observes its neighborhood N⁡(v)⊆UN(v)\subseteq U and must irrevocably either match vv to an unmatched vertex in N⁡(v)N(v) or leave vv unmatched.

We impose the following two structural assumptions.

  • •

    Interval neighborhoods. For every online vertex vv, its neighborhood N⁡(v)N(v) forms an interval on the ordered offline set UU. In other words, if offline vertices ui,uj∈N⁡(v)u_{i},u_{j}\in N(v) for some i<ji<j, then we also have uk∈N⁡(v)u_{k}\in N(v) for every k∈[i,j]k\in[i,j].

  • •

    Uniform-length. Every online vertex has exactly dd neighbors, where d≥2d\geq 2. Thus, for each v∈Vv\in V, the set N⁡(v)N(v) consists of dd consecutive offline vertices.

For an instance ℐ\mathcal{I} of the problem, let 𝖠𝖫𝖦⁡(ℐ)\mathsf{ALG}(\mathcal{I}) denote the size of the matching produced by an online algorithm, and let 𝖮𝖯𝖳⁡(ℐ)\mathsf{OPT}(\mathcal{I}) denote the size of a maximum matching. The competitive ratio of a possibly randomized online algorithm is

infℐ{𝔼⁡[𝖠𝖫𝖦⁡(ℐ)]𝖮𝖯𝖳⁡(ℐ)},\inf_{\mathcal{I}}\left\{\frac{\mathbb{E}[\mathsf{ALG}(\mathcal{I})]}{\mathsf{OPT}(\mathcal{I})}\right\},

where the expectation is taken over the internal randomness of the algorithm.

When the uniform-length assumption is dropped, so that |N⁡(v)||N(v)| may vary, we establish an upper bound of 1−1/e1-1/e on the competitive ratio of every online algorithm. The proof is given in Section 6.

We index the online vertices so that their neighborhoods are ordered from top to bottom. More precisely, for each i∈[n]i\in[n], let

si:=min⁡{j:uj∈N⁡(vi)}andli:=max⁡{j:uj∈N⁡(vi)},s_{i}:=\min\{j:u_{j}\in N(v_{i})\}\qquad\text{and}\qquad l_{i}:=\max\{j:u_{j}\in N(v_{i})\},

and relabel the online vertices so that s1≤s2≤⋯≤sns_{1}\leq s_{2}\leq\cdots\leq s_{n}, breaking ties arbitrarily. Since the neighborhood of each online vertex has length dd, we have li=si+d−1l_{i}=s_{i}+d-1 for every i∈[n]i\in[n]. Consequently, l1≤l2≤⋯≤lnl_{1}\leq l_{2}\leq\cdots\leq l_{n}. These indices do not necessarily reflect the online arrival order.

3 A Simple Randomized Algorithm: Flip

We now introduce a randomized algorithm, called Flip, that uses only one random bit. The algorithm chooses uniformly at random between the two natural priority orders on the offline vertices.

We call the deterministic rule used when flip=0\text{flip}=0 the up-matching rule, and the rule used when flip=1\text{flip}=1 the down-matching rule. For a graph GG and an arrival order σ\sigma, let 𝖠𝖫𝖦up​(G,σ)\mathsf{ALG}_{\mathrm{up}}(G,\sigma) denote the size of the matching produced by the up-matching rule, and let 𝖠𝖫𝖦down​(G,σ)\mathsf{ALG}_{\mathrm{down}}(G,\sigma) denote the corresponding quantity for the down-matching rule. Note that both 𝖠𝖫𝖦up​(G,σ)\mathsf{ALG}_{\mathrm{up}}(G,\sigma) and 𝖠𝖫𝖦down​(G,σ)\mathsf{ALG}_{\mathrm{down}}(G,\sigma) are deterministic, and we have

𝔼⁡[𝖠𝖫𝖦]=12⋅(𝖠𝖫𝖦up​(G,σ)+𝖠𝖫𝖦down​(G,σ)).\mathbb{E}[\mathsf{ALG}]=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\Big(\mathsf{ALG}_{\mathrm{up}}(G,\sigma)+\mathsf{ALG}_{\mathrm{down}}(G,\sigma)\Big).

3.1 A Semi-adaptive Adversary and Worst-case Arrival Orders

We make the standard assumption of an oblivious adversary. That is, the adversary can decide the graph and the arrival order, but cannot see the internal randomness, i.e., the flip variable, when designing the instance. Recall that Figure 1 gives simple instances on which either up-matching or down-matching matches only about half of the vertices. Therefore, Flip cannot achieve a ratio better than 1/21/2 against a fully adaptive adversary. Nevertheless, we show that its ratio is at least 2/32/3 when the adversary is semi-adaptive.

Specifically, we analyze the performance of Flip against the following semi-adaptive adversary.

  1. 1.

    The adversary, who knows the algorithm, chooses the graph GG.

  2. 2.

    The algorithm samples the variable flip∈{0,1}\text{flip}\in\{0,1\}.

  3. 3.

    After observing flip, the adversary chooses the arrival order of the online vertices.

Therefore, the adversary may choose one arrival order σ0\sigma_{0} when flip=0\text{flip}=0 and another arrival order σ1\sigma_{1} when flip=1\text{flip}=1. On a fixed graph GG, the expected matching size of Flip is thus

minσ0⁡{12⋅𝖠𝖫𝖦up​(G,σ0)}+minσ1⁡{12⋅𝖠𝖫𝖦down​(G,σ1)}.\min_{\sigma_{0}}\left\{\frac{1}{2}\cdot\mathsf{ALG}_{\mathrm{up}}(G,\sigma_{0})\right\}+\min_{\sigma_{1}}\left\{\frac{1}{2}\cdot\mathsf{ALG}_{\mathrm{down}}(G,\sigma_{1})\right\}.
Theorem 3.1.

Against the semi-adaptive adversary, Flip is 2​d−13​d−2\frac{2d-1}{3d-2}-competitive.

Before proving the theorem, we reduce the analysis of Flip to graphs in which some maximum matching covers every online vertex. We then construct a maximum matching and identify a worst-case arrival order for each of the two deterministic matching rules.

Notice that for either rule, inserting additional online vertices while preserving the relative order of the original vertices cannot decrease the final matching size. Inserting a single online vertex either has no effect or creates an alternating path. The path ends either at a previously unmatched offline vertex, increasing the matching size by one, or at a previously matched online vertex that becomes unmatched, leaving the matching size unchanged.

Let MM be a maximum matching of GG, and let W⊆VW\subseteq V be the set of online vertices covered by MM. Since MM is maximum, we have 𝖮𝖯𝖳⁡(G)=|W|=𝖮𝖯𝖳⁡(GW)\mathsf{OPT}(G)=|W|=\mathsf{OPT}(G_{W}). For any online arrival order σ\sigma, let σW\sigma_{W} be the subsequence obtained by deleting the vertices in V∖WV\setminus W. The preceding argument gives, for each rule r∈{up,down}r\in\{\mathrm{up},\mathrm{down}\}, 𝖠𝖫𝖦r​(G,σ)≥𝖠𝖫𝖦r​(GW,σW)\mathsf{ALG}_{r}(G,\sigma)\geq\mathsf{ALG}_{r}(G_{W},\sigma_{W}), and hence

minσ⁡{𝖠𝖫𝖦r​(G,σ)}≥minτ⁡{𝖠𝖫𝖦r​(GW,τ)},\min_{\sigma}\{\mathsf{ALG}_{r}(G,\sigma)\}\geq\min_{\tau}\{\mathsf{ALG}_{r}(G_{W},\tau)\},

where the second minimum ranges over all arrival orders of WW. Therefore, it suffices to prove Theorem 3.1 for graphs that admit a maximum matching covering all online vertices. Henceforth, we assume without loss of generality that 𝖮𝖯𝖳=|V|=n\mathsf{OPT}=|V|=n.

Recall that the online vertices are indexed so that s1≤s2≤⋯≤sns_{1}\leq s_{2}\leq\cdots\leq s_{n}. Since all interval neighborhoods have the same length, this also gives l1≤l2≤⋯≤lnl_{1}\leq l_{2}\leq\cdots\leq l_{n}. Consider running up-matching with arrival order v1,v2,…,vnv_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{n}. Let M⋆M^{\star} denote the resulting matching. This is precisely the greedy procedure for convex bipartite matching studied by Glover [18], which yields the following lemma. For completeness, we provide an alternative proof as follows.

Lemma 3.2.

M⋆M^{\star} is a maximum matching of GG.

Proof.

For a matching MM and an online vertex vv, we write M⁡(v)=uM(v)=u if (u,v)∈M(u,v)\in M, and M(v)=⊥M(v)=\bot if vv is unmatched by MM. Let there be a dummy online vertex v0v_{0} that has no offline neighbor. We show inductively that, for every i∈[0,n]i\in[0,n], there exists a maximum matching MM such that for any j∈[0,i]j\in[0,i], we have M⁡(vj)=M⋆​(vj)M(v_{j})=M^{\star}(v_{j}). Suppose the claim holds for i−1i-1, and consider the following cases:

  • •

    M⋆(vi)=⊥M^{\star}(v_{i})=\bot. Then every neighbor of viv_{i} is occupied by an edge of M⋆M^{\star} incident to a smaller-indexed online vertex. These edges also belong to MM, and MM must leave viv_{i} unmatched as well.

  • •

    M⋆​(vi)=uaM^{\star}(v_{i})=u_{a}, while M(vi)=⊥M(v_{i})=\bot. Because MM is maximum, uau_{a} must be matched in MM, say to vkv_{k}. Since uau_{a} is not matched to any of v1,…,vi−1v_{1},\ldots,v_{i-1}, we have k>ik>i. Replacing (vk,ua)(v_{k},u_{a}) by (vi,ua)(v_{i},u_{a}) preserves the size of the matching and makes M⁡(vi)=uaM(v_{i})=u_{a}.

  • •

    M⋆​(vi)=uaM^{\star}(v_{i})=u_{a} while M⁡(vi)=ubM(v_{i})=u_{b}, where a≠ba\neq b. The vertex ubu_{b} is not matched to any of v1,…,vi−1v_{1},\ldots,v_{i-1}. Since M⋆M^{\star} greedily chooses the smallest-indexed available neighbor of viv_{i}, we have a<ba<b. If uau_{a} is unmatched in MM, we may simply replace (vi,ub)(v_{i},u_{b}) by (vi,ua)(v_{i},u_{a}). Otherwise, let vkv_{k} (with k>ik>i) be matched to uau_{a}. Since ua∈N⁡(vk)u_{a}\in N(v_{k}), we have sk≤as_{k}\leq a. Together with a<ba<b and li≤lkl_{i}\leq l_{k}, we have

    sk≤a<b≤li≤lk,s_{k}\leq a<b\leq l_{i}\leq l_{k},

    and hence ub∈N⁡(vk)u_{b}\in N(v_{k}). We may therefore replace {(vi,ub),(vk,ua)}\{(v_{i},u_{b}),(v_{k},u_{a})\} by {(vi,ua),(vk,ub)}\{(v_{i},u_{a}),(v_{k},u_{b})\}.

Therefore, in every case, we obtain a maximum matching MM that satisfies M⁡(vi)=M⋆​(vi)M(v_{i})=M^{\star}(v_{i}). The lemma follows by induction. ∎

By the preceding reduction, M⋆M^{\star} covers every online vertex. By symmetry, the down-matching rule is optimal under the reverse order vn,vn−1,…,v1v_{n},v_{n-1},\ldots,v_{1}. The next lemma shows that each of these two orders is a worst-case order for the opposite rule (see Figure 1 for an example).

Lemma 3.3 (Worst-case Arrival Orders).

For every graph GG, we have

minσ⁡{𝖠𝖫𝖦up​(G,σ)}=𝖠𝖫𝖦up​(G,(vn,vn−1,…,v1)),\min_{\sigma}\left\{\mathsf{ALG}_{\mathrm{up}}(G,\sigma)\right\}=\mathsf{ALG}_{\mathrm{up}}\left(G,(v_{n},v_{n-1},\ldots,v_{1})\right),

and

minσ⁡{𝖠𝖫𝖦down​(G,σ)}=𝖠𝖫𝖦down​(G,(v1,v2,…,vn)).\min_{\sigma}\left\{\mathsf{ALG}_{\mathrm{down}}(G,\sigma)\right\}=\mathsf{ALG}_{\mathrm{down}}\left(G,(v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{n})\right).
Proof.

We prove the statement for the up-matching rule. The proof for the down-matching rule is symmetric. Let σ0=(vn,…,v1)\sigma_{0}=(v_{n},\ldots,v_{1}). Consider an arbitrary arrival order σ≠σ0\sigma\neq\sigma_{0}. Then σ\sigma contains two consecutively arriving vertices viv_{i} and vjv_{j} with i<ji<j. Let σ′\sigma^{\prime} be the arrival order obtained by swapping these two consecutive vertices in σ\sigma, so that vjv_{j} arrives immediately before viv_{i}. We show that this swap cannot increase the final matching size. More precisely, we have 𝖠𝖫𝖦up​(G,σ)≥𝖠𝖫𝖦up​(G,σ′)\mathsf{ALG}_{\mathrm{up}}(G,\sigma)\geq\mathsf{ALG}_{\mathrm{up}}(G,\sigma^{\prime}).

Since i<ji<j, we have li≤ljl_{i}\leq l_{j}. For vjv_{j}, neighbors in N⁡(vi)∩N⁡(vj)N(v_{i})\cap N(v_{j}) (if there is any) have higher priorities than those in N⁡(vj)∖N⁡(vi)N(v_{j})\setminus N(v_{i}). Immediately before viv_{i} and vjv_{j} arrive:

  • •

    If no vertex in N⁡(vi)∩N⁡(vj)N(v_{i})\cap N(v_{j}) is unmatched, or if at least one vertex in N⁡(vi)∖N⁡(vj)N(v_{i})\setminus N(v_{j}) is unmatched, the two resulting matchings under σ\sigma and σ′\sigma^{\prime} are identical.

  • •

    If at least two vertices in N⁡(vi)∩N⁡(vj)N(v_{i})\cap N(v_{j}) are unmatched, the resulting matchings differ only at viv_{i} and vjv_{j}, and we still have 𝖠𝖫𝖦up​(G,σ)=𝖠𝖫𝖦up​(G,σ′)\mathsf{ALG}_{\mathrm{up}}(G,\sigma)=\mathsf{ALG}_{\mathrm{up}}(G,\sigma^{\prime}).

The only remaining case is that all offline vertices in N⁡(vi)N(v_{i}) are already matched before viv_{i} and vjv_{j} arrive, except a unique vertex w0∈N⁡(vi)∩N⁡(vj)w_{0}\in N(v_{i})\cap N(v_{j}). In this case:

  • •

    Under order σ\sigma, viv_{i} arrives earlier and matches to w0w_{0}, vjv_{j} matches to the smallest-indexed unmatched offline vertex w1w_{1} in N⁡(vj)∖N⁡(vi)N(v_{j})\setminus N(v_{i}), if such w1w_{1} exists;

  • •

    Under order σ′\sigma^{\prime}, vjv_{j} arrives earlier and matches to w0w_{0}, viv_{i} is unmatched.

A standard alternating path argument gives 𝖠𝖫𝖦up​(G,σ)≥𝖠𝖫𝖦up​(G,σ′)\mathsf{ALG}_{\mathrm{up}}(G,\sigma)\geq\mathsf{ALG}_{\mathrm{up}}(G,\sigma^{\prime}). Repeatedly applying the above adjacent swaps transforms any arrival order into (vn,vn−1,…,v1)(v_{n},v_{n-1},\ldots,v_{1}) without increasing the matching size. Therefore, (vn,vn−1,…,v1)(v_{n},v_{n-1},\ldots,v_{1}) is a worst-case arrival order for the up-matching rule.

By reversing the order of the offline indices, the same argument shows that (v1,v2,…,vn)(v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{n}) is a worst-case arrival order for the down-matching rule. ∎

Having identified the worst arrival order for each rule, we next bound the total number of online vertices left unmatched by the two rules.

3.2 From Unmatched Vertices to Bad Indices

In this subsection, we introduce a discrete function ff, called the offset function, and relate the unmatched online vertices to certain one-sided local extrema of ff, which we call bad indices.

For each i∈[n]i\in[n], let μi∈[m]\mu_{i}\in[m] be the index of the offline vertex that gets matched to viv_{i} by M⋆M^{\star}. Recall that when viv_{i} is processed during the construction of M⋆M^{\star}, every offline vertex with index in [si,μi−1][s_{i},\mu_{i-1}] is already occupied whenever this interval is non-empty, while the vertex with index μi−1+1\mu_{i-1}+1 is available. Therefore, we have μ1=s1\mu_{1}=s_{1}, and μi=max⁡{si,μi−1+1}\mu_{i}=\max\{s_{i},\mu_{i-1}+1\} for every i∈[2,n]i\in[2,n].

Definition 3.4 (Offset Function).

For each online vertex viv_{i}, where i∈[n]i\in[n], define

f⁡(i):=μi−si+1.f(i):=\mu_{i}-s_{i}+1.

In other words, f⁡(i)f(i) is the number of neighbors of viv_{i} whose index is at most μi\mu_{i}; see Figure 2.

Since si≤μi≤li=si+d−1s_{i}\leq\mu_{i}\leq l_{i}=s_{i}+d-1, it follows immediately that f⁡(i)∈[d]f(i)\in[d]. The following lemma shows the one-sided Lipschitzness of ff.

Lemma 3.5 (ff is one-sided Lipschitz).

For every 1≤i<j≤n1\leq i<j\leq n, we have f⁡(j)−f⁡(i)≤j−if(j)-f(i)\leq j-i.

Proof.

The recurrence μi=max⁡{si,μi−1+1}\mu_{i}=\max\{s_{i},\mu_{i-1}+1\} implies that, for every i∈[2,n]i\in[2,n],

f⁡(i)=max⁡{si,μi−1+1}−si+1=max⁡{0,f⁡(i−1)−(si−si−1)}+1≤f⁡(i−1)+1,f(i)=\max\{s_{i},\mu_{i-1}+1\}-s_{i}+1=\max\{0,f(i-1)-(s_{i}-s_{i-1})\}+1\leq f(i-1)+1,

where the inequality follows from si≥si−1s_{i}\geq s_{i-1}. Consequently, for every i<ji<j,

f⁡(j)−f⁡(i)=∑k=i+1j(f⁡(k)−f⁡(k−1))≤j−i,f(j)-f(i)=\sum_{k=i+1}^{j}(f(k)-f(k-1))\leq j-i,

and the lemma follows. ∎

The Lipschitz property is one-sided: it limits how quickly ff can increase but imposes no similar restriction on how quickly it can decrease. For example, take two disjoint copies of the graph GG shown in Figure 2 and concatenate them in both the offline and online orders. At the boundary between the two copies, the offset function drops sharply from f⁡(10)=4f(10)=4 to f⁡(11)=1f(11)=1 in a single step.

Since each online vertex has dd neighbors, none of the first dd arrivals would be left unmatched by either of the two matching rules. The following two lemmas further establish the necessary conditions for an online vertex to be unmatched.

Lemma 3.6.

Consider any online vertex viv_{i} with i∈[d+1,n]i\in[d+1,n]. If it is not matched by the down-matching rule under the worst arrival order, then we must have

f⁡(i)>f⁡(j),∀j∈[i−d,i−1].f(i)>f(j),\qquad\forall j\in[i-d,i-1].
Proof.

Assume the contrary that there exists some j∈[i−d,i−1]j\in[i-d,i-1] such that f⁡(j)≥f⁡(i)f(j)\geq f(i). We show that viv_{i} must have an available neighbor upon arrival, contradicting the assumption that it is unmatched. Recall that lil_{i} (resp. ljl_{j}) is the largest index of a neighbor of viv_{i} (resp. vjv_{j}). Thus

lj=μj+d−f⁡(j),li=μi+d−f⁡(i).l_{j}=\mu_{j}+d-f(j),\qquad l_{i}=\mu_{i}+d-f(i).

Since f⁡(j)≥f⁡(i)f(j)\geq f(i), we have

li−lj=(μi−μj)+(f⁡(j)−f⁡(i))≥μi−μj≥i−j.l_{i}-l_{j}=(\mu_{i}-\mu_{j})+(f(j)-f(i))\geq\mu_{i}-\mu_{j}\geq i-j.

Immediately after vjv_{j} arrives, every offline vertex with index larger than ljl_{j} is unmatched, because no previously arrived online vertex is adjacent to it.

Next, we count the number of available neighbors of viv_{i} upon its arrival.

  • •

    If si>ljs_{i}>l_{j}, all matched neighbors of viv_{i} are matched by vertices that arrived between vjv_{j} and viv_{i}. Note that there are only i−j−1≤d−1i-j-1\leq d-1 such vertices, which implies that at least one neighbor of viv_{i} is not matched.

  • •

    If si≤ljs_{i}\leq l_{j}, then among neighbors with index [lj+1,li][l_{j}+1,l_{i}], at most i−j−1i-j-1 of them are matched, which implies that at least one of them is not matched, because li−lj≥i−jl_{i}-l_{j}\geq i-j.

Thus, at least one neighbor of viv_{i} is available when viv_{i} arrives, a contradiction. ∎

By symmetry, if viv_{i} is unmatched by the up-matching rule, then f⁡(i)f(i) is strictly smaller than the values at the next dd indices. The proof is omitted, as it is identical to that of Lemma 3.6 after reversing the order.

Lemma 3.7.

Consider any online vertex viv_{i} with i∈[1,n−d]i\in[1,n-d]. If it is not matched by the up-matching rule under the worst arrival order, then we must have

f⁡(i)<f⁡(j),∀j∈[i+1,i+d].f(i)<f(j),\qquad\forall j\in[i+1,i+d].

Lemma 3.6 and 3.7 identify two types of indices at which an unmatched online vertex may occur. We collect these indices in the following sets.

Definition 3.8 (Bad Indices).

Define

H\displaystyle H :={x∈[d+1,n]:f⁡(x)>maxy∈[x−d,x−1]⁡{f⁡(y)}},\displaystyle:=\left\{x\in[d+1,n]:f(x)>\max_{y\in[x-d,x-1]}\{f(y)\}\right\},
L\displaystyle L :={x∈[1,n−d]:f⁡(x)<miny∈[x+1,x+d]⁡{f⁡(y)}}.\displaystyle:=\left\{x\in[1,n-d]:f(x)<\min_{y\in[x+1,x+d]}\{f(y)\}\right\}.

An index in HH (resp. LL) is called an HH-bad (resp. LL-bad) index.

Notice that an index may belong to both HH and LL. For example, in Figure 2, we have H={5,6,7}H=\{5,6,7\} and L={4,5,6}L=\{4,5,6\}.

By Lemmas 3.6 and 3.7, every online vertex left unmatched by the down-matching rule has an HH-bad index, whereas every online vertex left unmatched by the up-matching rule has an LL-bad index. Equivalently,

{i∈[n]:vi​ is unmatched by the down-matching rule}⊆H,\displaystyle\{i\in[n]:v_{i}\text{ is unmatched by the down-matching rule}\}\subseteq H,
{i∈[n]:vi​ is unmatched by the up-matching rule}⊆L.\displaystyle\{i\in[n]:v_{i}\text{ is unmatched by the up-matching rule}\}\subseteq L.

Consequently, the expected matching size of Flip is lower-bounded by

12​((n−|H|)+(n−|L|))≥n−|H|+|L|2.\frac{1}{2}\left((n-|H|)+(n-|L|)\right)\geq n-\frac{|H|+|L|}{2}.

Recall that 𝖮𝖯𝖳=n\mathsf{OPT}=n. To prove Theorem 3.1, it suffices to establish the bound

|H|+|L|≤2​d−23​d−2⋅n.|H|+|L|\leq\frac{2d-2}{3d-2}\cdot n. (2)

4 Bounding the Number of Bad Indices

In this section, we bound |H|+|L||H|+|L|, the total number of bad indices, where an index that is both HH-bad and LL-bad is counted twice. Throughout, fix an arbitrary offset function f:[n]→[d]f:[n]\to[d] satisfying the one-sided Lipschitz condition, i.e., f⁡(i+1)≤f⁡(i)+1f(i+1)\leq f(i)+1 for every i∈[n−1]i\in[n-1]. These are the only properties of ff used in this section; in particular, we do not require that ff arises from a bipartite graph with uniform interval neighborhoods.

4.1 Maximal Chains

We first group the bad indices into maximal chains that are well separated.

Definition 4.1 (Maximal Chain).

List the HH-bad indices in increasing order. An HH-chain is a sequence C=(i1,i2,…,ix)C=(i_{1},i_{2},\ldots,i_{x}) of consecutive indices in this list such that ik+1−ik≤di_{k+1}-i_{k}\leq d for every k<xk<x. The chain is maximal if it cannot be extended by another HH-bad index on either side. Let 𝒞H\mathcal{C}_{H} be the collection of maximal HH-chains. We define LL-chains and the collection 𝒞L\mathcal{C}_{L} analogously.

For any maximal chain C=(i1,i2,…,ix)∈𝒞H∪𝒞LC=(i_{1},i_{2},\ldots,i_{x})\in\mathcal{C}_{H}\cup\mathcal{C}_{L}, we denote its starting index, ending index, and length by

start​(C)=i1,end​(C)=ix,len​(C)=x.\text{start}(C)=i_{1},\qquad\text{end}(C)=i_{x},\qquad\text{len}(C)=x.

The maximal chains partition HH and LL. In particular, we have

∑C∈𝒞Hlen​(C)=|H|,∑D∈𝒞Llen​(D)=|L|.\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}_{H}}\text{len}(C)=|H|,\qquad\sum_{D\in\mathcal{C}_{L}}\text{len}(D)=|L|.

Furthermore, maximal chains of the same type are separated by at least d+1d+1 indices. Specifically, for any C1,C2∈𝒞HC_{1},C_{2}\in\mathcal{C}_{H} with start​(C1)<start​(C2)\text{start}(C_{1})<\text{start}(C_{2}), we have

start​(C2)≥end​(C1)+d+1.\text{start}(C_{2})\geq\text{end}(C_{1})+d+1.

In other words, between the last index of C1C_{1} and the first index of C2C_{2}, there are at least dd other indices. We next record a basic property of maximal chains.

Lemma 4.2.

Let C=(i1,…,ix)C=(i_{1},\ldots,i_{x}) be any maximal chain. Then we have

x−1≤f⁡(ix)−f⁡(i1)≤min⁡{ix−i1,d−1}.x-1\leq f(i_{x})-f(i_{1})\leq\min\{i_{x}-i_{1},d-1\}. (3)
Proof.

By Definition 4.1, for every k<xk<x, we have ik+1−ik≤di_{k+1}-i_{k}\leq d, which implies f⁡(ik)<f⁡(ik+1)f(i_{k})<f(i_{k+1}). Because ff is integer-valued, we have f⁡(ik+1)−f⁡(ik)≥1f(i_{k+1})-f(i_{k})\geq 1. Summing over all k∈{1,…,x−1}k\in\{1,\ldots,x-1\} gives x−1≤f⁡(ix)−f⁡(i1)x-1\leq f(i_{x})-f(i_{1}). The final inequality in Equation (3) follows from the one-sided Lipschitz property of ff (Lemma 3.5) and from f⁡(⋅)∈[d]f(\cdot)\in[d]. ∎

Corollary 4.3.

For every C∈𝒞HC\in\mathcal{C}_{H} and D∈𝒞LD\in\mathcal{C}_{L}, we have

len​(C)≤d−f⁡(start​(C))+1, and len​(D)≤f⁡(end​(D)).\text{len}(C)\leq d-f(\text{start}(C))+1,\quad\text{ and }\quad\text{len}(D)\leq f(\text{end}(D)). (4)

Consequently, every maximal chain has length at most d−1d-1.

Proof.

For every C∈𝒞HC\in\mathcal{C}_{H}, Lemma 4.2 implies

len​(C)≤1+f⁡(end​(C))−f⁡(start​(C))≤1+d−f⁡(start​(C))≤d−1,\text{len}(C)\leq 1+f(\text{end}(C))-f(\text{start}(C))\leq 1+d-f(\text{start}(C))\leq d-1,

where the last inequality holds because start​(C)∈H\text{start}(C)\in H implies f​(start​(C))≥2f(\text{start}(C))\geq 2.

Similarly, for every D∈𝒞LD\in\mathcal{C}_{L}, Lemma 4.2 implies

len​(D)≤1+f⁡(end​(D))−f⁡(start​(D))≤f⁡(end​(D))≤d−1,\text{len}(D)\leq 1+f(\text{end}(D))-f(\text{start}(D))\leq f(\text{end}(D))\leq d-1,

where the last inequality holds because end​(D)∈L\text{end}(D)\in L implies f​(end​(D))≤d−1f(\text{end}(D))\leq d-1. ∎

We next show that if an LL-chain precedes an HH-chain and the two chains are sufficiently close, then their total length is bounded.

Lemma 4.4.

Let C∈𝒞HC\in\mathcal{C}_{H} and D∈𝒞LD\in\mathcal{C}_{L}. If 2≤start​(C)−end​(D)≤2​d2\leq\text{start}(C)-\text{end}(D)\leq 2d, then len​(C)+len​(D)≤d−1\text{len}(C)+\text{len}(D)\leq d-1.

Proof.

By the assumption of the lemma,

[end​(D)+1,end​(D)+d]∩[start​(C)−d,start​(C)−1]≠∅.[\text{end}(D)+1,\text{end}(D)+d]\cap[\text{start}(C)-d,\text{start}(C)-1]\neq\varnothing.

For any zz in this intersection, the definitions of LL-bad and HH-bad indices give

f⁡(end​(D))<f⁡(z)<f⁡(start​(C)).f(\text{end}(D))<f(z)<f(\text{start}(C)).

Since ff is integer-valued, f⁡(start​(C))≥f⁡(end​(D))+2f(\text{start}(C))\geq f(\text{end}(D))+2. Therefore, by Lemma 4.2,

len​(C)+len​(D)\displaystyle\text{len}(C)+\text{len}(D) ≤(1+f⁡(end​(C))−f⁡(start​(C)))+(1+f⁡(end​(D))−f⁡(start​(D)))\displaystyle\leq\bigl(1+f(\text{end}(C))-f(\text{start}(C))\bigr)+\bigl(1+f(\text{end}(D))-f(\text{start}(D))\bigr)
≤d+1+f⁡(end​(D))−f⁡(start​(C))\displaystyle\leq d+1+f(\text{end}(D))-f(\text{start}(C))
≤d−1,\displaystyle\leq d-1,

where the second inequality uses f​(end​(C))≤df(\text{end}(C))\leq d and f​(start​(D))≥1f(\text{start}(D))\geq 1. ∎

We use these properties of maximal chains to bound |H|+|L||H|+|L| in the following subsections.

4.2 Proxies: A Warm-up Analysis

As a warm-up, we first prove |H|≤d−12​d−1⋅n|H|\leq\frac{d-1}{2d-1}\cdot n; the symmetric argument gives the same bound for |L||L|.

Recall that |H|=∑C∈𝒞Hlen​(C)|H|=\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}_{H}}\text{len}(C). We upper bound |H||H| by the following charging argument. For each maximal chain C∈𝒞HC\in\mathcal{C}_{H}, we define a proxy P⁡(C)P(C), which is a subset of indices in [n][n]. We show that

  • (1)

    for each C∈𝒞HC\in\mathcal{C}_{H}, we have |P⁡(C)|≥2​d−1d−1⋅len​(C)|P(C)|\geq\frac{2d-1}{d-1}\cdot\text{len}(C);

  • (2)

    the proxies {P⁡(C)}C∈𝒞H\{P(C)\}_{C\in\mathcal{C}_{H}} are pairwise disjoint.

Combining these two properties, we get

2​d−1d−1⋅|H|=∑C∈𝒞H2​d−1d−1⋅len​(C)≤∑C∈𝒞H|P⁡(C)|≤n,\frac{2d-1}{d-1}\cdot|H|=\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}_{H}}\frac{2d-1}{d-1}\cdot\text{len}(C)\leq\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}_{H}}|P(C)|\leq n,

where the last inequality follows since the proxies are pairwise disjoint.

It remains to construct these proxies. For each C∈𝒞HC\in\mathcal{C}_{H}, we let

P⁡(C)=[start​(C)−d,end​(C)].P(C)=[\text{start}(C)-d,\text{end}(C)].

The proxy satisfies property (1) because

|P⁡(C)|=d+1+(end​(C)−start​(C))≥d+len​(C)≥2​d−1d−1⋅len​(C),|P(C)|=d+1+(\text{end}(C)-\text{start}(C))\geq d+\text{len}(C)\geq\frac{2d-1}{d-1}\cdot\text{len}(C),

where the second inequality follows from len​(C)≤d−1\text{len}(C)\leq d-1. Property (2) follows directly because any maximal HH-chain C′C^{\prime} preceding CC satisfies end​(C′)≤start​(C)−d−1\text{end}(C^{\prime})\leq\text{start}(C)-d-1.

Symmetrically, we can also show that |L|≤d−12​d−1⋅n|L|\leq\frac{d-1}{2d-1}\cdot n. Unfortunately, combining the two bounds gives only |H|+|L|≤2​d−22​d−1⋅n|H|+|L|\leq\frac{2d-2}{2d-1}\cdot n, which yields a competitive ratio approaching 1/21/2 as d→∞d\to\infty.

A key observation is that the two inequalities |H|≤d−12​d−1⋅n|H|\leq\frac{d-1}{2d-1}\cdot n and |L|≤d−12​d−1⋅n|L|\leq\frac{d-1}{2d-1}\cdot n cannot be tight simultaneously. For example, for the hard instance for down-matching in Figure 1, we have n=2​d−1n=2d-1 and |H|=d−1|H|=d-1. Hence |H|=d−12​d−1⋅n|H|=\frac{d-1}{2d-1}\cdot n. However, in this case L=∅L=\varnothing, which gives a strictly better bound on |H|+|L||H|+|L|. Similarly, for the hard instance for up-matching, we have |L|=d−12​d−1⋅n|L|=\frac{d-1}{2d-1}\cdot n but H=∅H=\varnothing. This suggests that we should design proxies simultaneously for maximal chains in 𝒞H\mathcal{C}_{H} and 𝒞L\mathcal{C}_{L}, and provide an upper bound for their combined size. Consider the naive combination of the proxies above for chains in 𝒞H\mathcal{C}_{H} and 𝒞L\mathcal{C}_{L}:

  • •

    let P⁡(C)=[start​(C)−d,end​(C)]P(C)=[\text{start}(C)-d,\text{end}(C)] for each C∈𝒞HC\in\mathcal{C}_{H};

  • •

    let Q⁡(D)=[start​(D),end​(D)+d]Q(D)=[\text{start}(D),\text{end}(D)+d] for each D∈𝒞LD\in\mathcal{C}_{L}.

While the proxies {P⁡(C)}C∈𝒞H\{P(C)\}_{C\in\mathcal{C}_{H}} are pairwise disjoint and the proxies {Q⁡(D)}D∈𝒞L\{Q(D)\}_{D\in\mathcal{C}_{L}} are pairwise disjoint, there may be overlaps between some P⁡(C)P(C) and Q⁡(D)Q(D). If there were no overlaps, the same charging argument would give |H|+|L|≤d−12​d−1⋅n|H|+|L|\leq\frac{d-1}{2d-1}\cdot n, which is false in general.

Consider an LL-chain DD preceding an HH-chain CC. Since Q⁡(D)Q(D) extends the interval of DD by a distance of dd to the right and P⁡(C)P(C) extends the interval of CC by a distance of dd to the left, if Q⁡(D)∩P⁡(C)≠∅Q(D)\cap P(C)\neq\varnothing, then the two chains must have a distance at most 2​d2d, i.e., start​(C)−end​(D)≤2​d\text{start}(C)-\text{end}(D)\leq 2d. However, in such a case, we can use Lemma 4.4 to show that the total length of CC and DD is at most d−1d-1. This interaction bound allows us to use shorter proxies than those defined above. Intuitively, when a chain is short, say len​(C)≤(d−1)/2\text{len}(C)\leq(d-1)/2, its proxy need not extend the chain by a full distance of dd. We can therefore shorten the proxies of short chains to reduce potential overlaps. Moreover, the proxy design should distinguish chains longer than (d−1)/2(d-1)/2 from those of length at most (d−1)/2(d-1)/2, since two long chains cannot interact in this way.

As a first target, consider proving |H|+|L|≤2​n/3|H|+|L|\leq 2n/3, which is equivalent to

3⋅|H|+3⋅|L|≤2⋅n.3\cdot|H|+3\cdot|L|\leq 2\cdot n.

Ideally, we want to design a proxy P⁡(C)P(C) for every C∈𝒞HC\in\mathcal{C}_{H} and a proxy Q⁡(D)Q(D) for every D∈𝒞LD\in\mathcal{C}_{L}, such that the following properties hold:

  • 1

    for each C∈𝒞HC\in\mathcal{C}_{H}, we have |P​(C)|≥3⋅len​(C)|P(C)|\geq 3\cdot\text{len}(C);

  • 2

    for each D∈𝒞LD\in\mathcal{C}_{L}, we have |Q​(D)|≥3⋅len​(D)|Q(D)|\geq 3\cdot\text{len}(D);

  • 3

    every index in [n][n] is covered at most twice by the proxies {P⁡(C)}C∈𝒞H∪{Q⁡(D)}D∈𝒞L\{P(C)\}_{C\in\mathcal{C}_{H}}\cup\{Q(D)\}_{D\in\mathcal{C}_{L}}.

If these three properties hold, the same counting argument gives |H|+|L|≤2​n/3|H|+|L|\leq{2n}/{3}. Two obstacles prevent such a direct construction.

First, observe that we cannot require the proxies {P⁡(C)}C∈𝒞H\{P(C)\}_{C\in\mathcal{C}_{H}} to be pairwise disjoint, as otherwise we can show that |H|≤n/3|H|\leq n/3, which is incorrect. Thus some overlap between the proxies is unavoidable. In particular, overlaps may occur not only between proxies of different types, as discussed above, but also between proxies of the same type.

Second, we may no longer be able to require P⁡(C)P(C) to be an ordinary subset of [n][n]. For an extreme example, consider the hard instance for down-matching in Figure 1. Here n=2​d−1n=2d-1, and the unique maximal HH-chain CC has length d−1d-1. Therefore, it is infeasible to have both P⁡(C)⊆[n]P(C)\subseteq[n] and |P​(C)|≥3⋅len​(C)|P(C)|\geq 3\cdot\text{len}(C), for any d≥3d\geq 3. Note that this can only happen when len​(C)>(d−1)/2\text{len}(C)>(d-1)/2. If len​(C)≤(d−1)/2\text{len}(C)\leq(d-1)/2, then the interval [start​(C)−d,end​(C)][\text{start}(C)-d,\text{end}(C)] has size at least d+len​(C)≥3⋅len​(C)d+\text{len}(C)\geq 3\cdot\text{len}(C), so it contains enough space for the proxy.

In summary, these observations suggest constructing proxies for HH- and LL-chains simultaneously and bounding their total size. The construction should distinguish different chain lengths and use two tracks to accommodate the larger proxies. Finally, strengthening the target bound from |H|+|L|≤2​n/3|H|+|L|\leq 2n/3 to |H|+|L|≤2​d−23​d−2⋅n|H|+|L|\leq\frac{2d-2}{3d-2}\cdot n requires one additional unit of proxy size per maximal chain.

4.3 A Two-Track Proxy Packing

We now present a two-track proxy packing motivated by the observations above.

Let κ:=|𝒞H|+|𝒞L|\kappa:=|\mathcal{C}_{H}|+|\mathcal{C}_{L}| be the total number of maximal chains. We prove that

3​(|H|+|L|)+κ≤2​n.3(|H|+|L|)+\kappa\leq 2n. (5)

The proof uses two copies of [n][n], called tracks. On the first track, every HH-chain receives a large proxy and every LL-chain receives a small proxy; on the second track, these roles are reversed. We show that the proxies on each track can be packed into [n][n] and that the two proxies assigned to each chain CC have total size 3⋅len​(C)+13\cdot\text{len}(C)+1. After the track labels are removed, every index of [n][n] is covered at most twice.

Before describing the construction, we show that Equation (5) implies the desired bound on |H|+|L||H|+|L|. By Corollary 4.3, every maximal chain has length at most d−1d-1. Therefore,

κ≥|H|+|L|d−1.\kappa\geq\frac{|H|+|L|}{d-1}.

Combining this inequality with (5) gives

3​(|H|+|L|)+|H|+|L|d−1≤2​n.3(|H|+|L|)+\frac{|H|+|L|}{d-1}\leq 2n.

Rearranging the inequality yields the desired upper bound:

|H|+|L|≤2​d−23​d−2⋅n.|H|+|L|\leq\frac{2d-2}{3d-2}\cdot n.

We next construct the proxies, beginning with the first track. For every C∈𝒞HC\in\mathcal{C}_{H}, define its proxy as

P⁡(C):={[start​(C)−d,start​(C)−d+3⋅len​(C)],len​(C)≤(d−1)/2,[start​(C)−d,start​(C)+len​(C)−1],len​(C)>(d−1)/2.P(C):=\begin{cases}[\text{start}(C)-d,\text{start}(C)-d+3\cdot\text{len}(C)],&\text{len}(C)\leq(d-1)/2,\\ [\text{start}(C)-d,\text{start}(C)+\text{len}(C)-1],&\text{len}(C)>(d-1)/2.\end{cases}

We call a chain CC short if len​(C)≤(d−1)/2\text{len}(C)\leq(d-1)/2, and long otherwise.

  • •

    When CC is short, the proxy has size 3⋅len​(C)+13\cdot\text{len}(C)+1.

  • •

    When CC is long, the proxy has size len​(C)+d\text{len}(C)+d.

Thus |P​(C)|=p​(len​(C))|P(C)|=p(\text{len}(C)), where p⁡(x):=min⁡{3​x+1,d+x}p(x):=\min\{3x+1,d+x\}. Moreover, P⁡(C)⊆[n]P(C)\subseteq[n]: we have start​(C)≥d+1\text{start}(C)\geq d+1, and the last index of P⁡(C)P(C) is at most end​(C)\text{end}(C).

Our goal is to assign two proxies to each chain CC whose combined size is 3⋅len​(C)+13\cdot\text{len}(C)+1. For short CC, the proxy P⁡(C)P(C) we construct above already has size 3⋅len​(C)+13\cdot\text{len}(C)+1, which means that its proxy in the second track is empty. For long CC, the proxy P⁡(C)P(C) has size len​(C)+d<3⋅len​(C)+1\text{len}(C)+d<3\cdot\text{len}(C)+1, which means that its proxy in the second track should have size 2⋅len​(C)−d+12\cdot\text{len}(C)-d+1. Since the roles of HH and LL are reversed on the second track, the first-track proxy for an LL-chain should follow the same rule as the second-track proxy for an HH-chain.

Therefore, for every D∈𝒞LD\in\mathcal{C}_{L}, we define its proxy as

Q⁡(D):={∅,len​(D)≤(d−1)/2,[end​(D)+d−len​(D)+1,end​(D)+len​(D)+1],len​(D)>(d−1)/2.Q(D):=\begin{cases}\varnothing,&\text{len}(D)\leq(d-1)/2,\\ [\text{end}(D)+d-\text{len}(D)+1,\text{end}(D)+\text{len}(D)+1],&\text{len}(D)>(d-1)/2.\end{cases} (6)

Thus |Q​(D)|=q​(len​(D))|Q(D)|=q(\text{len}(D)), where q⁡(x):=max⁡{0,2​x−d+1}q(x):=\max\{0,2x-d+1\}. Moreover, Q⁡(D)⊆[n]Q(D)\subseteq[n]: since end​(D)≤n−d\text{end}(D)\leq n-d and len​(D)≤d−1\text{len}(D)\leq d-1, its right endpoint is at most nn.

The key step is to show that the total size of the first-track proxies is at most nn.

Lemma 4.5 (First-track Packing).

We have

∑C∈𝒞Hp⁡(len​(C))+∑D∈𝒞Lq⁡(len​(D))≤n.\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}_{H}}p(\text{len}(C))+\sum_{D\in\mathcal{C}_{L}}q(\text{len}(D))\leq n. (7)

We defer the proof to the next subsection and now construct the second-track proxies symmetrically. Importantly, for every x∈[d−1]x\in[d-1], we have p⁡(x)+q⁡(x)=3​x+1p(x)+q(x)=3x+1.

We define the second track proxies based on a rotated version of ff. Specifically, we define

f←​(i):=d+1−f⁡(n+1−i).\overleftarrow{f}(i):=d+1-f(n+1-i).

Geometrically, f←\overleftarrow{f} is obtained by rotating ff by 180 degrees, reversing both the horizontal and vertical directions. For i≤ji\leq j, we have

f←​(j)−f←​(i)=f⁡(n+1−i)−f⁡(n+1−j)≤j−i.\overleftarrow{f}(j)-\overleftarrow{f}(i)=f(n+1-i)-f(n+1-j)\leq j-i.

Thus f←\overleftarrow{f} satisfies the same one-sided Lipschitz condition. Moreover, the map i↦n+1−ii\mapsto n+1-i exchanges the HH-chains and the LL-chains without changing their lengths. For example, every C∈𝒞HC\in\mathcal{C}_{H} for ff becomes an LL-chain for f←\overleftarrow{f}. Applying the same construction to f←\overleftarrow{f} therefore gives

∑C∈𝒞Hq⁡(len​(C))+∑D∈𝒞Lp⁡(len​(D))≤n.\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}_{H}}q(\text{len}(C))+\sum_{D\in\mathcal{C}_{L}}p(\text{len}(D))\leq n. (8)

Here 𝒞H\mathcal{C}_{H} and 𝒞L\mathcal{C}_{L} continue to denote the chains of the original function ff.

Adding (7) and (8), and using p⁡(x)+q⁡(x)=3​x+1p(x)+q(x)=3x+1, gives

∑C∈𝒞H(3⋅len​(C)+1)+∑D∈𝒞L(3⋅len​(D)+1)=3​(|H|+|L|)+κ≤2​n.\displaystyle\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}_{H}}\bigl(3\cdot\text{len}(C)+1\bigr)+\sum_{D\in\mathcal{C}_{L}}\bigl(3\cdot\text{len}(D)+1\bigr)=3(|H|+|L|)+\kappa\leq 2n.

This proves (5) and yields the following main result.

Theorem 4.6.

For every offset function f:[n]→[d]f:[n]\to[d] satisfying the one-sided Lipschitz condition, we have

|H|+|L|≤2​d−23​d−2⋅n.|H|+|L|\leq\frac{2d-2}{3d-2}\cdot n.

Consequently, Flip is 2​d−13​d−2\frac{2d-1}{3d-2}-competitive against the semi-adaptive adversary.

4.4 Upper Bounding the Total Size of Proxies

We now prove Lemma 4.5, which states that the total size of the first-track proxies is at most nn. If all proxies were disjoint, the result would be immediate. The proxies may overlap, so the key is to control these overlaps and eliminate them without changing the total proxy size.

Our analysis has three main steps:

  • •

    We first show that proxies of the same type are pairwise disjoint (see Lemma 4.7). Consequently, overlap can only happen between proxies of different types.

  • •

    Then we show that every proxy can overlap with at most one other proxy, which is of a different type, in Lemma 4.9. This implies that we can group overlapping proxies into pairs.

  • •

    Finally, for every overlapping pair, we relocate one proxy without changing its size so that the resulting proxies are pairwise disjoint.

Recall that for any C∈𝒞HC\in\mathcal{C}_{H}, its proxy is defined as

P⁡(C)={[start​(C)−d,start​(C)−d+3⋅len​(C)],len​(C)≤(d−1)/2,[start​(C)−d,start​(C)+len​(C)−1],len​(C)>(d−1)/2.P(C)=\begin{cases}[\text{start}(C)-d,\text{start}(C)-d+3\cdot\text{len}(C)],&\text{len}(C)\leq(d-1)/2,\\ [\text{start}(C)-d,\text{start}(C)+\text{len}(C)-1],&\text{len}(C)>(d-1)/2.\end{cases}

Define P~​(C):=[start​(C)−d,start​(C)+len​(C)−1]\tilde{P}(C):=[\text{start}(C)-d,\text{start}(C)+\text{len}(C)-1] as the extended proxy of CC. It can be verified that regardless of whether CC is short or long, we always have P​(C)⊆P~​(C)P(C)\subseteq\tilde{P}(C).

Also recall that the proxy of every D∈𝒞LD\in\mathcal{C}_{L} is defined as

Q⁡(D)={∅,len​(D)≤(d−1)/2,[end​(D)+d−len​(D)+1,end​(D)+len​(D)+1],len​(D)>(d−1)/2.Q(D)=\begin{cases}\varnothing,&\text{len}(D)\leq(d-1)/2,\\ [\text{end}(D)+d-\text{len}(D)+1,\text{end}(D)+\text{len}(D)+1],&\text{len}(D)>(d-1)/2.\end{cases}

Define Q~​(D):=[start​(D),end​(D)+d]\tilde{Q}(D):=[\text{start}(D),\text{end}(D)+d] as the extended proxy of DD. Then Q​(D)⊆Q~​(D)Q(D)\subseteq\tilde{Q}(D).

We prove a statement stronger than disjointness of proxies of the same type: we show that even their extended versions are disjoint.

Lemma 4.7.

The extended proxies of the same type are pairwise disjoint.

Proof.

Consider any C∈𝒞HC\in\mathcal{C}_{H}. Note that the last index of P~​(C)\tilde{P}(C) is

start​(C)+len​(C)−1≤end​(C),\text{start}(C)+\text{len}(C)-1\leq\text{end}(C),

which is smaller than start​(C′)−d\text{start}(C^{\prime})-d for the succeeding HH-chain by maximality. Therefore, the extended proxies of the HH-chains are pairwise disjoint.

Now we consider any D∈𝒞LD\in\mathcal{C}_{L}. The last index of Q~​(D)\tilde{Q}(D) is end​(D)+d\text{end}(D)+d, which is smaller than start​(D′)\text{start}(D^{\prime}) for any succeeding LL-chain by maximality. Hence, the extended proxies of the LL-chains are also pairwise disjoint. ∎

The lemma also implies that, for chains of the same type, the order of the extended proxies agrees with the order of the chains. Consequently, only proxies of different types may overlap. Next, we show that if two proxies of different types overlap, then the HH-chain is short and the LL-chain is long.

Lemma 4.8.

Suppose P⁡(C)∩Q⁡(D)≠∅P(C)\cap Q(D)\neq\varnothing, where C∈𝒞HC\in\mathcal{C}_{H} and D∈𝒞LD\in\mathcal{C}_{L}. Then we have len​(C)+len​(D)≤d−1\text{len}(C)+\text{len}(D)\leq d-1. Furthermore, CC is short, and DD is long.

Proof.

Let x:=len​(C)x:=\text{len}(C) and y:=len​(D)y:=\text{len}(D). Since P⁡(C)P(C) intersects Q⁡(D)Q(D), the left endpoint of Q⁡(D)Q(D) is at most the right endpoint of P⁡(C)P(C). Consequently,

end​(D)+d−y+1≤start​(C)−d−1+min⁡{3​x+1,d+x},\text{end}(D)+d-y+1\leq\text{start}(C)-d-1+\min\{3x+1,d+x\},

which implies

end​(D)−start​(C)≤x+y−d−2.\text{end}(D)-\text{start}(C)\leq x+y-d-2. (9)

We first show that end​(D)<start​(C)\text{end}(D)<\text{start}(C). Otherwise, by the one-sided Lipschitz property (Lemma 3.5) and Corollary 4.3,

x+y≤d+1+f⁡(end​(D))−f⁡(start​(C))≤d+1+end​(D)−start​(C),x+y\leq d+1+f(\text{end}(D))-f(\text{start}(C))\leq d+1+\text{end}(D)-\text{start}(C),

contradicting Equation (9). Therefore start​(C)>end​(D)\text{start}(C)>\text{end}(D). We further rule out start​(C)−end​(D)=1\text{start}(C)-\text{end}(D)=1. In this case, since end​(D)∈L\text{end}(D)\in L and start​(C)=end​(D)+1\text{start}(C)=\text{end}(D)+1, the definition of an LL-bad index gives f​(end​(D))<f​(start​(C))f(\text{end}(D))<f(\text{start}(C)). Corollary 4.3 then implies

x+y≤d+1+f⁡(end​(D))−f⁡(start​(C))≤d.x+y\leq d+1+f(\text{end}(D))-f(\text{start}(C))\leq d.

On the other hand, Equation (9) gives x+y≥d+1x+y\geq d+1, a contradiction. Thus start​(C)−end​(D)≥2\text{start}(C)-\text{end}(D)\geq 2.

Again, since P⁡(C)P(C) intersects Q⁡(D)Q(D), the left endpoint of P⁡(C)P(C) is at most the right endpoint of Q⁡(D)Q(D). Thus

start​(C)−d≤end​(D)+y+1.\text{start}(C)-d\leq\text{end}(D)+y+1.

Consequently, we have

start​(C)−end​(D)≤d+y+1≤2​d,\text{start}(C)-\text{end}(D)\leq d+y+1\leq 2d,

where the last inequality follows from y≤d−1y\leq d-1. Lemma 4.4 therefore gives x+y≤d−1x+y\leq d-1. Finally, Q⁡(D)≠∅Q(D)\neq\varnothing implies that DD is long and 2​y≥d2y\geq d. Together with x+y≤d−1x+y\leq d-1, this gives x≤(d−2)/2x\leq(d-2)/2, so CC is short. ∎

We next show that no proxy can overlap two distinct proxies.

Lemma 4.9.

Every proxy overlaps with at most one other proxy.

Proof.

Suppose first that a proxy P⁡(C)P(C) intersects two proxies Q⁡(D1)Q(D_{1}) and Q⁡(D2)Q(D_{2}), where start​(D1)<start​(D2)\text{start}(D_{1})<\text{start}(D_{2}). Let x:=len​(C)x:=\text{len}(C), y1:=len​(D1)y_{1}:=\text{len}(D_{1}) and y2:=len​(D2)y_{2}:=\text{len}(D_{2}). By Lemma 4.8, CC is short, so |P⁡(C)|=3​x+1|P(C)|=3x+1, and both D1D_{1} and D2D_{2} are long. Recall that Q⁡(D1)Q(D_{1}) ends at end​(D1)+y1+1\text{end}(D_{1})+y_{1}+1 and Q⁡(D2)Q(D_{2}) starts at end​(D2)+d−y2+1\text{end}(D_{2})+d-y_{2}+1. An interval meeting both Q⁡(D1)Q(D_{1}) and Q⁡(D2)Q(D_{2}) must have size at least

1+(end​(D2)+d−y2+1)−(end​(D1)+y1+1)≥2​d−y1+1,1+\left(\text{end}(D_{2})+d-y_{2}+1\right)-\left(\text{end}(D_{1})+y_{1}+1\right)\geq 2d-y_{1}+1,

where the inequality holds since end​(D2)−y2≥end​(D1)+d\text{end}(D_{2})-y_{2}\geq\text{end}(D_{1})+d, by maximality. Hence 3​x≥2​d−y13x\geq 2d-y_{1}.

On the other hand, Lemma 4.8 gives x+y1≤d−1x+y_{1}\leq d-1, and therefore

y1≤d−1−2​d−y13,y_{1}\leq d-1-\frac{2d-y_{1}}{3},

which implies y1≤(d−3)/2y_{1}\leq(d-3)/2, contradicting that D1D_{1} is long.

Conversely, suppose that a proxy Q⁡(D)Q(D) intersects two proxies P⁡(C1)P(C_{1}) and P⁡(C2)P(C_{2}), where start​(C1)<start​(C2)\text{start}(C_{1})<\text{start}(C_{2}). Let x1:=len​(C1)x_{1}:=\text{len}(C_{1}) and x2:=len​(C2)x_{2}:=\text{len}(C_{2}). By Lemma 4.8, both C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} are short, and DD is long. Similarly, an interval meeting both P⁡(C1)P(C_{1}) and P⁡(C2)P(C_{2}) must have size at least

1+(start​(C2)−d)−(start​(C1)−d+3​x1)≥d−2​x1+1,1+\left(\text{start}(C_{2})-d\right)-\left(\text{start}(C_{1})-d+3x_{1}\right)\geq d-2x_{1}+1, (10)

where the inequality holds because start​(C2)≥start​(C1)+x1+d\text{start}(C_{2})\geq\text{start}(C_{1})+x_{1}+d. However, since DD is long and x1+len​(D)≤d−1x_{1}+\text{len}(D)\leq d-1, the proxy Q⁡(D)Q(D) has size

2⋅len​(D)−d+1≤2⋅(d−1−x1)−d+1≤d−2​x1−1,2\cdot\text{len}(D)-d+1\leq 2\cdot(d-1-x_{1})-d+1\leq d-2x_{1}-1,

contradicting Equation (10). ∎

We now combine these ingredients to prove Lemma 4.5.

Proof of Lemma 4.5: Recall that our goal is to show that the total size of the first-track proxies is at most nn. Lemma 4.7 shows that only proxies of different types can overlap, and Lemma 4.9 implies that if two proxies P⁡(C)P(C) and Q⁡(D)Q(D) overlap, they are disjoint from any other proxies. For each overlapping pair, we relocate Q⁡(D)Q(D) so that all proxies become pairwise disjoint while preserving their total size.

Consider an overlap between P⁡(C)P(C) and Q⁡(D)Q(D), and let x:=len​(C)x:=\text{len}(C) and y:=len​(D)y:=\text{len}(D). By Lemma 4.8, CC is short and DD is long. When CC is short, its proxy P⁡(C)P(C) is a proper subinterval of the extended proxy P~​(C)\tilde{P}(C). Specifically, P⁡(C)P(C) and P~​(C)\tilde{P}(C) have the same starting position, while their ending positions differ by

(start​(C)+x−1)−(start​(C)−d+3​x)=d−2​x−1.\left(\text{start}(C)+x-1\right)-\left(\text{start}(C)-d+3x\right)=d-2x-1.

Since DD is long and x+y≤d−1x+y\leq d-1, we have

|Q⁡(D)|=2​y−d+1≤2⋅(d−1−x)−d+1≤d−2​x−1.|Q(D)|=2y-d+1\leq 2\cdot(d-1-x)-d+1\leq d-2x-1.

Therefore, we can shift Q⁡(D)Q(D) to immediately follow P⁡(C)P(C) inside P~​(C)\tilde{P}(C). We do this for every overlapping pair of P⁡(C)P(C) and Q⁡(D)Q(D). Since the extended proxies P~​(C)\tilde{P}(C) are pairwise disjoint, it remains to show that P~​(C)∖P​(C)\tilde{P}(C)\setminus P(C) is disjoint from every QQ-proxy other than Q⁡(D)Q(D).

Assume for contradiction that Q⁡(D′)Q(D^{\prime}), where D′≠DD^{\prime}\neq D, overlaps with P~​(C)∖P​(C)\tilde{P}(C)\setminus P(C). Then Q⁡(D′)Q(D^{\prime}) cannot have been relocated; otherwise, it would lie inside some P~​(C′)\tilde{P}(C^{\prime}), which is disjoint from P~​(C)\tilde{P}(C). Since Q⁡(D)Q(D) overlaps with P⁡(C)P(C) (before relocation), Q⁡(D′)Q(D^{\prime}) is disjoint from P⁡(C)P(C). Because the QQ-proxies are pairwise disjoint and appear in the same order as their chains, Q⁡(D′)Q(D^{\prime}) can overlap P~​(C)∖P​(C)\tilde{P}(C)\setminus P(C) only if DD precedes D′D^{\prime}. Its starting index must then lie in P~​(C)∖P​(C)\tilde{P}(C)\setminus P(C) (see Figure 4). Let y′:=len​(D′)y^{\prime}:=\text{len}(D^{\prime}).

By maximality, we have end​(D′)−y′≥end​(D)+d\text{end}(D^{\prime})-y^{\prime}\geq\text{end}(D)+d. Then the starting index of Q⁡(D′)Q(D^{\prime}) satisfies

end​(D′)+d−y′+1\displaystyle\text{end}(D^{\prime})+d-y^{\prime}+1 ≥end​(D)+2​d+1\displaystyle\geq\text{end}(D)+2d+1
≥(start​(C)−d−y−1)+2​d+1\displaystyle\geq(\text{start}(C)-d-y-1)+2d+1
=start​(C)+(d−y)\displaystyle=\text{start}(C)+(d-y)
≥start​(C)+x+1,\displaystyle\geq\text{start}(C)+x+1,

where the second inequality holds because the ending index of Q⁡(D)Q(D) is at least the starting index of P⁡(C)P(C), and the last inequality follows from x+y≤d−1x+y\leq d-1. This is a contradiction, because the starting index of Q⁡(D′)Q(D^{\prime}) is strictly larger than the ending index of P~​(C)\tilde{P}(C).  

5 Tightness and Impossibility Results

In this section, we complement the competitive guarantee for Flip with two upper bounds.

5.1 Tightness of Flip

We first give an instance showing that the competitive analysis of Flip is tight for every d≥2d\geq 2.

Theorem 5.1.

For every integer d≥2d\geq 2, there exists an instance on which Flip has competitive ratio 2​d−13​d−2\frac{2d-1}{3d-2}. In particular, this ratio converges to 2/32/3 as d→∞d\to\infty.

Construction of the Hard Instance.

Fix an integer d≥2d\geq 2, and consider an instance with 3​d−23d-2 offline vertices U={u1,…,u3​d−2}U=\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{3d-2}\} and equally many online vertices V={v1,…,v3​d−2}V=\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{3d-2}\}. The neighborhoods of the online vertices are defined by

N⁡(vi)={{ui,ui+1,…,ui+d−1},i∈{1,…,d−1},{ud,ud+1,…,u2​d−1},i∈{d,…,2​d−1},{ui−d+1,ui−d+2,…,ui},i∈{2​d,…,3​d−2}.N(v_{i})=\begin{cases}\{u_{i},u_{i+1},\ldots,u_{i+d-1}\},&i\in\{1,\ldots,d-1\},\\ \{u_{d},u_{d+1},\ldots,u_{2d-1}\},&i\in\{d,\ldots,2d-1\},\\ \{u_{i-d+1},u_{i-d+2},\ldots,u_{i}\},&i\in\{2d,\ldots,3d-2\}.\end{cases}

The left graph in Figure 2 illustrates this construction for d=4d=4.

Consider the arrival order

v1,…,vd−1,v2​d,…,v3​d−2,vd,…,v2​d−1.v_{1},\ldots,v_{d-1},\quad v_{2d},\ldots,v_{3d-2},\quad v_{d},\ldots,v_{2d-1}.

Under either matching rule used by Flip, all 2​d−22d-2 vertices in the first two blocks are matched. At that point, exactly one vertex in {ud,ud+1,…,u2​d−1}\{u_{d},u_{d+1},\ldots,u_{2d-1}\} remains unmatched: it is udu_{d} under one rule and u2​d−1u_{2d-1} under the other. Since every vertex in the final block has this set as its neighborhood, the first such vertex is matched to the unique remaining offline vertex, while the other d−1d-1 vertices remain unmatched. Consequently,

𝖠𝖫𝖦up=𝖠𝖫𝖦down=2​d−1.\mathsf{ALG}_{\mathrm{up}}=\mathsf{ALG}_{\mathrm{down}}=2d-1.

On the other hand, the instance admits the perfect matching {(ui,vi):i∈[3​d−2]}\{(u_{i},v_{i}):i\in[3d-2]\}, and hence 𝖮𝖯𝖳=3​d−2\mathsf{OPT}=3d-2. This gives the claimed upper bound.

5.2 A 3/43/4 Upper Bound for Any Algorithm

In this subsection, we show that no randomized online algorithm can achieve a competitive ratio strictly larger than 3/43/4.

Construction of the Hard Instance.

Assume that dd is even. Let kk be an even integer and let n=k​dn=kd. Partition the offline set U={u1,…,un}U=\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{n}\} into kk consecutive blocks U1,…,UkU_{1},\ldots,U_{k}, each of size dd. We further divide each block UiU_{i} into two half-blocks:

Ui,1\displaystyle U_{i,1} :={u(i−1)​d+1,…,u(i−1)​d+d/2},\displaystyle:=\{u_{(i-1)d+1},\ldots,u_{(i-1)d+d/2}\},
Ui,2\displaystyle U_{i,2} :={u(i−1)​d+d/2+1,…,ui​d},\displaystyle:=\{u_{(i-1)d+d/2+1},\ldots,u_{id}\},

and write Ui=Ui,1∪Ui,2U_{i}=U_{i,1}\cup U_{i,2}.

The online vertices arrive in two phases. The first phase is common to both realizations of the instance. For every i∈[k]i\in[k], let there be d/2d/2 online vertices whose neighborhood is UiU_{i}.

After the first phase, one of the following two continuations is selected uniformly at random.

  • •

    In the odd continuation, for every i∈{1,3,…,k−1}i\in\{1,3,\ldots,k-1\}, there are dd online vertices whose neighborhood is Ui,2∪Ui+1,1U_{i,2}\cup U_{i+1,1}.

  • •

    In the even continuation, there are d/2d/2 online vertices whose neighborhood is U1U_{1}, d/2d/2 online vertices whose neighborhood is UkU_{k}, and, for every i∈{2,4,…,k−2}i\in\{2,4,\ldots,k-2\}, there are dd online vertices whose neighborhood is Ui,2∪Ui+1,1U_{i,2}\cup U_{i+1,1}.

Thus, each realization contains n/2n/2 online vertices in each phase, and every online neighborhood is an interval of exactly dd consecutive offline vertices; see Figure 5 for an illustration with k=4k=4.

Theorem 5.2.

No randomized online algorithm has a competitive ratio strictly larger than 3/43/4.

Proof.

We first analyze an arbitrary deterministic online algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A}. For each i∈[k]i\in[k], let aia_{i} and bib_{i} denote the numbers of vertices in Ui,1U_{i,1} and Ui,2U_{i,2} that are matched by 𝒜\mathcal{A} during the first phase. Let

m:=∑i=1k(ai+bi).m:=\sum_{i=1}^{k}(a_{i}+b_{i}).

Since the first phase contains n/2n/2 online vertices, m≤n/2m\leq n/2.

Let 𝒜odd\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{odd}} and 𝒜even\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{even}} be the matching sizes obtained under the two continuations, respectively. In the odd continuation, the number of offline vertices still available in Ui,2∪Ui+1,1U_{i,2}\cup U_{i+1,1} is d−bi−ai+1d-b_{i}-a_{i+1}. Consequently,

𝒜odd≤m+∑1≤i≤k−1i​ odd(d−bi−ai+1).\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{odd}}\leq m+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq i\leq k-1\\ i\text{ odd}\end{subarray}}(d-b_{i}-a_{i+1}).

Similarly, the two endpoint groups in the even continuation contain dd online vertices in total, while each internal group can match at most the number of available vertices in its neighborhood. Hence,

𝒜even≤m+d+∑2≤i≤k−2i​ even(d−bi−ai+1).\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{even}}\leq m+d+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}2\leq i\leq k-2\\ i\text{ even}\end{subarray}}(d-b_{i}-a_{i+1}).

Averaging these two inequalities gives

𝒜odd+𝒜even2\displaystyle\frac{\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{odd}}+\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{even}}}{2} ≤m+12​(n−∑i=1k−1(bi+ai+1))=m+12​(n−m+a1+bk)\displaystyle\leq m+\frac{1}{2}\left(n-\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}(b_{i}+a_{i+1})\right)=m+\frac{1}{2}(n-m+a_{1}+b_{k})
=n2+m2+a1+bk2≤3​n4+d2=(34+12​k)⋅n,\displaystyle=\frac{n}{2}+\frac{m}{2}+\frac{a_{1}+b_{k}}{2}\leq\frac{3n}{4}+\frac{d}{2}=\left(\frac{3}{4}+\frac{1}{2k}\right)\cdot n,

where the last inequality follows from m≤n/2m\leq n/2 and a1,bk≤d/2a_{1},b_{k}\leq d/2.

On the other hand, both realizations admit a perfect matching:

  • •

    For the odd continuation, match the second-phase vertices to Ui,2∪Ui+1,1U_{i,2}\cup U_{i+1,1} for every odd ii, and match the first-phase vertices associated with UiU_{i} to Ui,1U_{i,1} when ii is odd and to Ui,2U_{i,2} when ii is even.

  • •

    For the even continuation, match the two endpoint groups to U1,1U_{1,1} and Uk,2U_{k,2}, respectively. Match every internal second-phase group to its entire neighborhood, and match each first-phase group to the remaining half of its block.

Therefore, we have 𝖮𝖯𝖳=n\mathsf{OPT}=n for both realizations.

The preceding bound holds for every deterministic algorithm under the uniform distribution over the two continuations. By Yao’s minimax principle, for every randomized online algorithm, at least one realization in the support satisfies

𝔼⁡[𝖠𝖫𝖦]𝖮𝖯𝖳≤34+12​k.\frac{\mathbb{E}[\mathsf{ALG}]}{\mathsf{OPT}}\leq\frac{3}{4}+\frac{1}{2k}.

Since kk can be arbitrarily large, the desired upper bound of 3/43/4 follows. ∎

6 Without the Uniform-Length Assumption

In this section, we show that convexity alone is insufficient for beating the competitive ratio of 1−1/e1-1/e. More precisely, we prove the following theorem.

Theorem 6.1.

No algorithm has a competitive ratio strictly larger than 1−1/e1-1/e for online matching in convex bipartite graphs.

It suffices to prove the upper bound for deterministic fractional algorithms: the edge-matching probabilities of any randomized algorithm induce a deterministic fractional algorithm with the same ratio.

Recall the classic upper-triangular instance of Karp et al. [21] for general online bipartite matching. Starting with all offline vertices, the adversary repeatedly introduces one online vertex adjacent to the current set and then removes the least-matched offline vertex from all future neighborhoods. Unfortunately, the resulting graph is not convex: the removal of the least-matched offline vertex splits the offline vertices into two disconnected segments. Our main idea is to replace each vertex with sufficiently many copies, so that the neighborhoods are still intervals after some offline vertices are removed.

6.1 The Hard Instance

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be an arbitrary deterministic fractional algorithm. Fix an integer m≥1m\geq 1, and let UU be an ordered set of m!m! offline vertices. For every k∈[m]k\in[m] and every interval I⊆UI\subseteq U of size k!k!, we define the following recursive procedure 𝖡𝗎𝗂𝗅𝖽⁡(I,k)\mathsf{Build}(I,k). The hard instance is generated by 𝖡𝗎𝗂𝗅𝖽⁡(U,m)\mathsf{Build}(U,m).

  • •

    If k=1k=1, the procedure introduces one online vertex whose neighborhood is the unique vertex in II.

  • •

    For k≥2k\geq 2, partition II into kk consecutive subintervals I1,I2,…,IkI_{1},I_{2},\ldots,I_{k}, each containing (k−1)!(k-1)! offline vertices. Introduce (k−1)!(k-1)! online vertices, each with neighborhood II. We refer to them as the level-kk online vertices. After 𝒜\mathcal{A} processes these vertices, let λu\lambda_{u} denote the current matched fraction of each u∈Iu\in I. Choose an index r∈[k]r\in[k] such that

    ∑u∈Irλu=min⁡∑u∈Ijj∈[k]⁡λu,\sum_{u\in I_{r}}\lambda_{u}=\min_{j\in[k]}\sum_{u\in I_{j}}\lambda_{u},

    breaking ties arbitrarily. No future online vertex is adjacent to any vertex in IrI_{r}; we call IrI_{r} the dropped interval. For every j≠rj\neq r, recursively apply 𝖡𝗎𝗂𝗅𝖽⁡(Ij,k−1)\mathsf{Build}(I_{j},k-1).

Every online neighborhood produced by the construction is an interval in the given order of UU. Moreover, the instance admits a perfect matching of size m!m!. Indeed, at every recursive call, the level-kk online vertices can be matched to the dropped interval IrI_{r}, whose vertices have no future online neighbors. Therefore, we have 𝖮𝖯𝖳=m!\mathsf{OPT}=m!.

6.2 Bounding the Fractional Matching

We upper-bound the fractional matching size of 𝒜\mathcal{A} by tracking the (average) matched fraction within each recursive interval.

First, suppose that 𝒜\mathcal{A} distributes every online level uniformly over its neighboring interval. Suppose an invocation 𝖡𝗎𝗂𝗅𝖽⁡(I,k)\mathsf{Build}(I,k) begins with matched fraction xx on every vertex of II, and let wk​(x)w_{k}(x) denote the final average matched fraction after matching the online vertices at level kk. Clearly, we have w1​(x)=1w_{1}(x)=1. For k≥2k\geq 2, the level-kk online vertices raise the average matched fraction in II to x^=min⁡{1,x+1/k}\hat{x}=\min\{1,x+1/k\}. One of the kk subintervals is then dropped with average matched fraction x^\hat{x}, while the other k−1k-1 subintervals continue with the same average matched fraction. Therefore,

wk​(x)=x^k+k−1k⋅wk−1​(x^).w_{k}(x)=\frac{\hat{x}}{k}+\frac{k-1}{k}\cdot w_{k-1}(\hat{x}).

Unrolling this recurrence gives

wk​(x)=1k⋅∑l=1kmin⁡{1,x+∑s=lk1s}.w_{k}(x)=\frac{1}{k}\cdot\sum_{l=1}^{k}\min\left\{1,x+\sum_{s=l}^{k}\frac{1}{s}\right\}.

Notice that wkw_{k} is concave and non-decreasing. Moreover, wk​(x)−xw_{k}(x)-x is non-increasing.

We next show that wk​(x)w_{k}(x) upper-bounds the final average matched fraction in 𝖡𝗎𝗂𝗅𝖽⁡(I,k)\mathsf{Build}(I,k) even when the allocation across subintervals is nonuniform.

Lemma 6.2.

Consider an invocation 𝖡𝗎𝗂𝗅𝖽⁡(I,k)\mathsf{Build}(I,k) that begins with average matched fraction xx over the vertices in II. The final average matched fraction in II is at most wk​(x)w_{k}(x).

Proof.

We prove by induction on k≥1k\geq 1. The claim is immediate for k=1k=1, since the final matched fraction of the unique offline vertex is at most 1=w1​(x)1=w_{1}(x).

Now suppose that k≥2k\geq 2. After the level-kk online vertices have been processed, let y¯\bar{y} and yjy_{j} be the average matched fraction in II and IjI_{j} (where j∈[k]j\in[k]), respectively. Since level kk contains (k−1)!(k-1)! online vertices whereas |I|=k!|I|=k!, it can increase the average load in II by at most 1/k1/k. Hence, y¯≤min⁡{1,x+1/k}=x^\bar{y}\leq\min\left\{1,x+1/k\right\}=\hat{x}.

Let IrI_{r} be the dropped subinterval. By definition, we have yr=minj∈[k]⁡yj≤y¯y_{r}=\min_{j\in[k]}y_{j}\leq\bar{y}.

The dropped subinterval IrI_{r} contributes (k−1)!⋅yr(k-1)!\cdot y_{r} to the final matching. By the induction hypothesis, every remaining k−1k-1 subinterval IjI_{j} contributes at most (k−1)!⋅wk−1​(yj)(k-1)!\cdot w_{k-1}(y_{j}). Thus, the final average matched fraction in II is at most

1k​(yr+∑j≠rwk−1​(yj)).\frac{1}{k}\left(y_{r}+\sum_{j\neq r}w_{k-1}(y_{j})\right). (11)

By the concavity of wk−1w_{k-1} and yr≤y¯y_{r}\leq\bar{y},

yr+∑j≠rwk−1​(yj)\displaystyle y_{r}+\sum_{j\neq r}w_{k-1}(y_{j}) =yr+∑j=1kwk−1​(yj)−wk−1​(yr)\displaystyle=y_{r}+\sum_{j=1}^{k}w_{k-1}(y_{j})-w_{k-1}(y_{r})
≤y¯+∑j=1kwk−1​(yj)−wk−1​(y¯)≤y¯+(k−1)⋅wk−1​(y¯),\displaystyle\leq\bar{y}+\sum_{j=1}^{k}w_{k-1}(y_{j})-w_{k-1}(\bar{y})\leq\bar{y}+(k-1)\cdot w_{k-1}(\bar{y}),

where the first inequality holds because wk−1​(x)−xw_{k-1}(x)-x is non-increasing. The last expression is non-decreasing in y¯\bar{y}. Therefore, the quantity in Equation (11) is at most

x^k+k−1k⋅wk−1​(x^)=wk​(x),\frac{\hat{x}}{k}+\frac{k-1}{k}\cdot w_{k-1}(\hat{x})=w_{k}(x),

which completes the induction. ∎

Now we can prove Theorem 6.1.

Proof of Theorem 6.1: Consider the instance generated by 𝖡𝗎𝗂𝗅𝖽⁡(U,m)\mathsf{Build}(U,m). Initially, every offline vertex has zero matched fraction. Recall that 𝖮𝖯𝖳=m!\mathsf{OPT}=m!. By Lemma 6.2, the competitive ratio of any deterministic fractional algorithm in this instance is upper-bounded by

wm​(0)=1m​∑ℓ=1mmin⁡{1,∑s=ℓm1s}.w_{m}(0)=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{\ell=1}^{m}\min\left\{1,\sum_{s=\ell}^{m}\frac{1}{s}\right\}.

As m→∞m\to\infty, view ℓ/m\ell/m as x∈(0,1]x\in(0,1]. The harmonic sum ∑s=ℓm1/s\sum_{s=\ell}^{m}1/s converges to −ln⁡x-\ln x, and the preceding expression converges to

limm→∞wm​(0)=∫01min⁡{1,−ln⁡x}​𝑑x=∫01/e1​𝑑x+∫1/e1(−ln⁡x)​𝑑x=1−1e,\displaystyle\lim_{m\to\infty}w_{m}(0)=\int_{0}^{1}\min\{1,-\ln x\}\mathrm{d}x=\int_{0}^{1/e}1\mathrm{d}x+\int_{1/e}^{1}(-\ln x)\mathrm{d}x=1-\frac{1}{e},

and the theorem follows.
